label: Phaedo · Opposites and Recollection
title: Opposites and Recollection
paragraphs: When Socrates had said this, Cebes took it up. Socrates, he said, the rest seems to me well said, but what you say about the soul people find very hard to believe. They fear that when it parts from the body it no longer exists anywhere, but is destroyed and perishes on the very day the person dies, the moment it parts from the body; that as it comes out it is scattered like breath or smoke, and goes flying off and is gone, and is no longer anything anywhere. For if it did exist somewhere, gathered together by itself and rid of those evils you went through just now, there would be great hope, and a fine one, Socrates, that what you say is true. But this very point perhaps needs no little persuasion and proof: that the soul exists when the person has died, and has some power and wisdom.
That's true, Cebes, said Socrates. But what are we to do? Do you want us to talk these very things through, and see whether it is likely to be so or not?
I for one, said Cebes, would gladly hear what belief you hold about them.

I certainly do not think, said Socrates, that anyone who heard me now, not even if he were a comic poet, would say that I am chattering and talking about things that are no concern of mine. So if you agree, we must look into it thoroughly.

Let us examine it in some such way as this: whether the souls of people who have died are in Hades or not. Now there is an old story, which we remember, that they are there, having come from here, and that they come back here again and come to be from the dead. And if this is so, that the living come to be again from those who have died, must our souls not exist there? For they could hardly come to be again if they did not exist; and it would be sufficient proof that this is so, if it really became plain that the living come to be from nowhere else than from the dead. But if that is not so, some other argument would be needed.
Very much so, said Cebes.

Then do not look at this only in the case of human beings, he said, if you want to understand it more easily, but in the case of all animals and plants too; and in short, for all things that have a coming to be, let us see whether they all come to be in this way: opposites from nowhere else than from their opposites, wherever they happen to have such a thing — as the beautiful is, I suppose, opposite to the ugly, and just to unjust, and there are countless others like these. So let us examine this: whether whatever has an opposite must come to be from nowhere else than from its own opposite. For example, when something comes to be larger, it must, I suppose, come to be larger afterward from having been smaller before?
Yes.
And if it comes to be smaller, it will come to be smaller later from having been larger before?
That is so, he said.
And the weaker surely comes from the stronger, and the faster from the slower?
Certainly.
And again: if something comes to be worse, is it not from better, and if more just, from more unjust?
Of course.
Then we have this well enough, he said: that all things come to be in this way, opposite things from opposites?
Certainly.

And again: is there something like this in them too, that between every pair of opposites, since they are two, there are two comings to be, from the one to the other, and back again from the other to the first? Between a larger thing and a smaller there is increase and decrease, and so we call the one increasing and the other decreasing?
Yes, he said.

And so with separating and combining, and cooling and heating, and all the rest: even if in some cases we have no names for them, still in fact it must be so everywhere, that they come to be from each other and that there is a coming to be of each into the other?
Very much so, he said.
Well then, he said, is there an opposite to living, as sleeping is to being awake?
Very much so, he said.
What?
Being dead, he said.
Then these come to be from each other, if they are opposites, and since they are two, the comings to be between them are two?
Of course.

Then I will tell you one of the two pairs I was speaking of just now, said Socrates, both the pair and its comings to be; and you tell me the other. I say that the one is sleeping and the other being awake, and that being awake comes to be from sleeping and sleeping from being awake, and that their comings to be are falling asleep for the one and waking up for the other. Is that enough for you, he said, or not?
Very much so.
Then you tell me in the same way, he said, about life and death. Do you not say that being dead is the opposite of living?
I do.
And that they come to be from each other?
Yes.
Then from what is living, what is it that comes to be?
What is dead, he said.
And from what is dead? he said.
It must be agreed, he said, that it is what is living.
Then it is from the dead, Cebes, that living things and living people come to be?
It appears so, he said.
Then our souls exist in Hades, he said.
So it seems.
And of the two comings to be here, one is in fact plain? For dying is plain enough, is it not?
Very much so, he said.
What shall we do, then? he said. Shall we not supply the opposite coming to be to balance it, but leave nature lame on this side? Or must we give dying some opposite coming to be?
By all means, he said.
What is it?
Coming back to life.
Then, he said, if there is such a thing as coming back to life, this would be a coming to be from the dead into the living, this coming back to life?
Certainly.

So we are agreed in this way too that the living have come to be from the dead no less than the dead from the living; and if that is so, it seemed to be sufficient proof, I think, that the souls of the dead must exist somewhere, from where they come to be again.
It seems to me, Socrates, he said, that from what has been agreed it must be so.

Then look at it this way, Cebes, he said, and you will see that we were not wrong to agree, as it seems to me. For if the one set of things did not always balance the other as they come to be, going round as it were in a circle, but the coming to be were a straight line from the one only to its opposite, and did not bend back again to the other or make a turn, do you know that in the end all things would have the same shape, and be in the same condition, and would stop coming to be?
What do you mean? he said.

It is not hard to understand what I mean, he said. For example, if there were falling asleep, but waking up did not balance it by coming to be from what is asleep, you know that in the end everything would make Endymion seem a trifle, and he would be nowhere to be seen, because everything else would be in the same condition as he, asleep. And if all things were combined and never separated, the saying of Anaxagoras would soon have come true: ‘all things together.’ In the same way, my dear Cebes, if everything that has a share of life were to die, and when it had died the dead remained in that shape and did not come back to life again, is it not quite necessary that in the end all things would be dead and nothing alive? For if living things came to be from the other things, and the living things died, what means is there to keep everything from being used up into death?
None at all, it seems to me, Socrates, said Cebes. I think what you say is entirely true.

It is so, Cebes, he said, as it seems to me, beyond all doubt, and we are not deceived in agreeing to these very things. There really is such a thing as coming back to life, and the living do come to be from the dead, and the souls of the dead do exist, and it is better for the good ones and worse for the bad.

And besides, Socrates, Cebes took it up, there is that argument, if it is true, which you are in the habit of stating often, that our learning is in fact nothing other than recollection. According to this too we must, I suppose, have learned at some earlier time what we now recollect. But that is impossible unless our soul existed somewhere before it came to be in this human form. So in this way too the soul seems to be something immortal.
But Cebes, Simmias took it up, what are the proofs of this? Remind me, for I don't remember very well at the moment.

By one argument, said Cebes, and a very fine one: when people are questioned, if someone questions them well, they say for themselves how everything is — and yet if knowledge and a right account were not in them, they would not be able to do this. Then, if one takes them to diagrams or anything else of that kind, there it is shown most plainly that this is so.
But if you are not persuaded that way, Simmias, said Socrates, see whether you agree when you look at it like this. For you do find it hard to believe that what is called learning is recollection?

It is not that I disbelieve you, said Simmias. But I need to have happen to me the very thing the argument is about: to be reminded. And from what Cebes set out to say I already almost remember, and am persuaded. All the same I would like to hear now how you set out to say it.
Like this, he said. We agree, I suppose, that if anyone is to be reminded of something, he must have known it at some time before.
Certainly, he said.

Then do we also agree on this: that when knowledge comes to someone in a certain way, it is recollection? In what way do I mean? This. If someone sees one thing, or hears it, or takes it in by some other sense, and not only knows that thing but also thinks of another, the knowledge of which is not the same but different, are we not right to say that he was reminded of the thing he came to think of?
What do you mean?
For example: knowledge of a person, I suppose, is different from knowledge of a lyre.
Of course.

Then do you know that lovers, when they see a lyre or a cloak or anything else that the boy they love is in the habit of using, have this happen to them: they know the lyre, and they take into their thought the form of the boy whose lyre it was? And that is recollection. In the same way someone who sees Simmias is often reminded of Cebes, and there must be countless other cases like these.
Countless indeed, by Zeus, said Simmias.
Then, he said, is that sort of thing a kind of recollection? And most of all when it happens to someone with things he had already forgotten through time and not attending to them?
Very much so, he said.
And again, he said: is it possible on seeing a painted horse or a painted lyre to be reminded of a person, and on seeing Simmias painted to be reminded of Cebes?
Certainly.
And also on seeing Simmias painted to be reminded of Simmias himself?
It is indeed, he said.
Then does it not follow from all this that recollection comes from things that are like, and also from things that are unlike?
It follows.

But when someone is reminded of something by things that are like it, must this not happen to him as well: he thinks about whether or not this thing falls short at all, in its likeness, of the thing he was reminded of?
It must be, he said.

Then consider, he said, whether this is so. We say, I suppose, that there is something equal — I do not mean a stick equal to a stick or a stone to a stone or anything else of that kind, but something different beyond all these, the equal itself. Are we to say that it is something, or nothing?
We are to say it is, by Zeus, said Simmias, most certainly.
And do we know what it is?
Certainly, he said.

Where did we get the knowledge of it? Was it not from the things we were just speaking of: from seeing sticks or stones or other things that are equal, we came from these to think of that, which is different from them? Or does it not appear different to you? Look at it this way too. Do not equal stones and sticks, while staying the same, sometimes appear equal to one person and not to another?
Very much so.
And again: did the equals themselves ever appear to you unequal, or equality inequality?
Never, Socrates.
Then these equal things, he said, and the equal itself are not the same.
Not at all, it appears to me, Socrates.
And yet it is from these equal things, he said, different as they are from that equal, that you have nevertheless come to think of it and got the knowledge of it?
That's very true, he said.
Whether it is like them or unlike?
Certainly.
It makes no difference, he said. So long as, on seeing one thing, you come from that sight to think of another, whether like or unlike, it must have been recollection.
Very much so.

And again, he said: does something like this happen to us with the equals in the sticks and in the other equal things we were just speaking of? Do they appear to us to be equal in the same way as that which is equal itself, or do they fall short of it at all in being such as the equal is, or not at all?
They fall short by a great deal, he said.

Then we agree that when someone sees something and thinks: This thing that I now see wants to be like some other thing among the things that are, but falls short and cannot be such as that is, and is inferior — the one who thinks this must, I suppose, have known beforehand the thing he says it resembles but falls short of?
It must be.
Well then? Has something like that happened to us too, or not, with the equal things and the equal itself?
Entirely so.
Then we must have known the equal before that time when we first saw equal things and thought that all these strive to be like the equal, but fall short of it.
That is so.

But we also agree on this: that we have not come to think of it, and that it is not possible to think of it, from anywhere else than from seeing or touching or some other of the senses. I count all these as the same.
They are the same, Socrates, at least for what the argument means to show.
But then it is from the senses that we must come to think that all the things in the senses strive for that which is equal, and fall short of it. Or how do we say?
Just so.

Then before we began to see and hear and perceive in the other ways, we must, I suppose, have got knowledge of the equal itself, what it is, if we were going to refer the equal things from the senses to it, and think that all such things are eager to be like it but are inferior to it.
It must be, Socrates, from what has been said.
Now, as soon as we were born we were seeing and hearing and had the other senses?
Certainly.
But we must, we say, have got the knowledge of the equal before these?
Yes.
Then it seems we must have got it before we were born.
So it seems.

Then if we got it before we were born and were born having it, we knew, both before we were born and as soon as we were born, not only the equal and the larger and the smaller but all things of that kind? For our argument now is no more about the equal than about the beautiful itself, and the good itself, and the just, and the holy, and, as I say, about everything on which we set this seal, ‘the thing itself, what it is,’ both in our questions when we ask and in our answers when we answer. So we must have got the knowledge of all these before we were born.
That is so.

And if, having got it, we have not each time forgotten it, we must always be born knowing and always know throughout life. For to know is this: having got knowledge of something, to have it and not to have lost it. Or is that not what we call forgetting, Simmias — the loss of knowledge?
Surely it is, Socrates, he said.

But if, I think, we got it before we were born and lost it in being born, and later, by using our senses about these things, we get back those pieces of knowledge we once had before, would not what we call learning be getting back knowledge that is our own? And we would be right, I suppose, to call this recollecting?
Certainly.

For this at least appeared possible: that on perceiving something, whether by seeing or hearing or taking it in by some other sense, one thinks from it of something else that one had forgotten, to which it was near, being either unlike it or like. So, as I say, one of two things: either we were all born knowing them and know them throughout life, or those we say are learning are afterward only recollecting, and learning would be recollection.
That is very much so, Socrates.
Then which do you choose, Simmias? That we were born knowing, or that we recollect afterward things we had got knowledge of before?
I can't choose at the moment, Socrates.
Well, can you choose this, and what do you think about it? Would a man who knows be able to give an account of what he knows, or not?
He most certainly must, Socrates, he said.
And do you think everyone is able to give an account of the things we were speaking of just now?
I wish they could, said Simmias. But I am much more afraid that by this time tomorrow there will no longer be any human being able to do it worthily.
So you do not think, Simmias, he said, that everyone knows them?
Not at all.
Then they recollect what they once learned?
It must be.
When did our souls get the knowledge of them? Surely not since we were born as human beings.
Of course not.
Earlier, then.
Yes.
Then our souls existed before as well, Simmias, before they were in human form, apart from bodies, and they had wisdom.
Unless we get these pieces of knowledge at the moment of being born, Socrates; for that time is still left.

Very well, my friend. But at what other time do we lose them? For we are certainly not born having them, as we agreed just now. Or do we lose them at the very time we get them? Or can you name some other time?
Not at all, Socrates. I did not notice that I was talking nonsense.

Then is this how it stands for us, Simmias? he said. If the things we are always talking about exist, a beautiful and a good and all such being, and we refer everything from the senses to this, finding again that it existed before and was ours, and compare these things to it, then just as these exist, so our soul too must exist even before we were born. But if these do not exist, this argument will have been stated in vain? Is that how it stands, and is it equally necessary that these things exist and that our souls did, even before we were born, and if not the one, then not the other?

It seems to me overwhelmingly, Socrates, said Simmias, that the necessity is the same, and the argument takes refuge in a fine place: that our soul exists before we are born in the same way as the being you now speak of. For I have nothing so clear to me as this, that all such things exist as fully as anything can, a beautiful and a good and all the others you were speaking of just now. And to me it seems sufficiently proved.
And what about Cebes? said Socrates. For Cebes must be persuaded too.

Sufficiently, said Simmias, as I think; and yet he is the most stubborn of people in distrusting arguments. But I think he is fully persuaded of this, that our soul existed before we were born. Whether it will still exist after we die, however, does not seem even to me to have been proved, Socrates, he said. What Cebes said just now still stands in the way, the fear most people have, that at the moment the person dies the soul may be scattered and this may be the end of its existence. For what prevents it from coming to be and being put together from somewhere else, and existing before it ever arrives in a human body, and then, when it has arrived and parts from it, coming to an end itself and being destroyed?

Well said, Simmias, said Cebes. For it appears that half, as it were, of what is needed has been proved: that our soul existed before we were born. It must also be proved that it will exist after we die no less than before we were born, if the proof is to be complete.

It has been proved even now, Simmias and Cebes, said Socrates, if you are willing to put this argument together with the one we agreed on before it, that everything living comes to be from what is dead. For if the soul exists before as well, and if, when it goes into life and comes to be, it must come to be from nowhere else than from death and being dead, how must it not exist after it dies too, since it has to come to be again? So what you speak of has been proved even now.

Still, I think you and Simmias would gladly work through this argument even further, and that you have the fear children have, that the wind really does blow the soul apart and scatter it as it comes out of the body, especially when someone happens to die not in calm weather but in a high wind.

And Cebes laughed. Try to persuade us out of it, Socrates, he said, as if we were afraid. Or rather, not as if we were afraid; but perhaps there is a child in us too who fears such things. Try to change his mind, then, so that he does not fear death as he would the bogeymen.
Then you must sing a charm over him every day, said Socrates, until you have charmed him out of it.
Then where, Socrates, he said, shall we find a good charmer for such things, now that you are leaving us?

Greece is large, Cebes, he said, and there are surely good men in it, and the foreign peoples are many too. You must search through all of them looking for such a charmer, sparing neither money nor trouble, since there is nothing on which you could spend money to better purpose. And you must also search among yourselves, together; for perhaps you would not easily find anyone better able to do this than you.
That shall be done, said Cebes. But let us go back to where we left off, if that pleases you.
It does please me. How could it not?

divergences.older: not even if he were one of my old enemies, the Comic poets
divergences.lectio: not even if he were a comic poet
divergences.note: Socrates says only 'a comic poet'. Jowett's 'old enemies' is a gloss pointing back to Aristophanes and the Apology; the reader who has just read the Apology hears the echo without it.

divergences.phrase: τῷ μὲν ἴσα φαίνεται, τῷ δ’ οὔ
divergences.older: appear at one time equal, and at another time unequal
divergences.lectio: sometimes appear equal to one person and not to another
divergences.note: Jowett follows the other manuscript reading, 'at one time, at another'. Burnet's text has the dative, which can mean 'to one person and not to another' or 'equal to one thing and not to another'. The edition takes it of persons, which fits 'did they ever appear to you' in the next question.

divergences.phrase: μὴ δεδιέναι τὸν θάνατον ὥσπερ τὰ μορμολύκεια
divergences.older: him too we must persuade not to be afraid when he is alone in the dark
divergences.lectio: so that he does not fear death as he would the bogeymen
divergences.note: The dark is Jowett's. Plato's child fears death the way children fear the mormolykeia, the masks and monsters nurses frightened them with, and Cebes asks Socrates, not 'us', to talk him out of it.
